title: Sensor-agnostic own-signature/EM COP fusion as a TAK plugin, with disconnected tactical spectrum management (JRFL, assignments, interference tickets) and emitter-library distribution to cheap sensor fleets
problem: Brigade and division CEMA cells and spectrum managers are receiving heterogeneous cheap spectrum sensors (S2AS kits, MOTH, Dragonfly, TLS-BCT manpacks) whose detections do not fuse into one government-owned, DDIL-tolerant electromagnetic picture inside TAK/EWPMT-X, while frequency plans, JRFLs and interference reports still depend on reach-back to DISA enterprise tools (Spectrum XXI/JSDR/EMBM-J).

user.exact_role: Brigade/division CEMA section chief and EW technician (170A/17E), brigade and division Electromagnetic Spectrum Manager (Army MOS 25E; USMC 0681-type spectrum managers), EW platoon leader in the Multifunctional Reconnaissance Company; secondary: JFMO/JEMSO cell staff
user.echelon: Brigade combat team and division main/tactical command posts; secondary corps/JTF JEMSO cell

current_workflow: EW platoon and command-post staff run vendor sensors (S2AS kit, TLS-BCT manpack, MOTH, Dragonfly, ad hoc SDRs) and read each vendor's own GUI or laptop app.
Detections and own-emission observations are relayed by voice/chat or typed into ATAK as Cursor-on-Target points; screenshots go into PowerPoint for the commander's update.

The 25E spectrum manager compares observed emitters against frequency assignments exported from Spectrum XXI/JSDR (SFAF records) and against the JRFL built per CJCSM 3320.01D, usually in spreadsheets when disconnected.
Interference (EMI) reports arrive by voice/chat; the spectrum manager triages manually against assignments and EW schedules and re-enters results into Spectrum XXI/JSDR when connectivity returns.
The CEMA officer builds the EM overlay in EWPMT/Raven Claw (being replaced by EWPMT-X on TAK) or by hand; higher echelons receive the picture hours later.
Sensor signal-of-interest libraries are updated per vendor through proprietary tools or reprogramming-center channels, not through a common distribution mechanism.
current_solution: Own-signature: S2AS (3dB Labs, production contract June 2026, UCA pathway, 9 systems delivered by late Aug 2026, 46 planned by July 2027). Threat/EW picture: TLS-BCT manpack (Mastodon Design/CACI, ~$100M award July 2024) with its own visualization; EWPMT/Raven Claw (Raytheon lineage) being re-hosted as EWPMT-X on TAK with USMC. Spectrum management: DISA Spectrum XXI/JSDR/GEMSIS and the cloud EMBM-J (initial features Dec 2023; EMBM-J Decision Support launched Apr 2025 with a Palantir-built prototype). Workarounds: spreadsheets, chat, PowerPoint, ad hoc ATAK plugins (Parsons TEMS, CTIC TAKX-RF, open-source ATAKRR).
failure: At the seam between many vendor sensor feeds and the government-owned TAK/EWPMT-X picture: no common detection schema or time-aligned fusion across S2AS, TLS-BCT, REWSI sensors and ad hoc SDRs; no offline-first tactical client for assignments/JRFL/EMI tickets that later syncs to JSDR/EMBM-J; and no cross-vendor mechanism to push updated signal libraries to cheap sensor fleets under DDIL. The government now owns the framework (TAK) but has not yet contracted anyone specifically to own the sensor-agnostic fusion logic (the EWPMT-X integrator is not public).

evidence.claim: Army cancelled the EWPMT RS3 task-order follow-on in April 2024 citing evolving requirements, and is re-hosting EW planning and spectrum management on the TAK framework (EWPMT-X) with USMC, targeting replacement of EWPMT by FY2026.

evidence.label: FACT

evidence.claim: Army awarded 3dB Labs a ~$6.1M, 14-month OTA for the S2AS prototype (Apr 2025) and then a potential five-year $350M production contract (June 2026) under the Urgent Capability Acquisition pathway; nine systems were delivered within three weeks by late Aug 2026 with 46 expected by July 2027. Ceiling, not revenue; deliveries are early.

why_existing_startups_havent_solved: Sensor companies (Heaviside, RII, Distributed Spectrum, Anduril Pulsar/Lattice, 3dB Labs) monetize hardware plus their own visualization and have no incentive to build a vendor-neutral fusion layer; the government host only became fixed when the Army declared TAK the EWPMT-X framework in 2024, and the EWPMT-X integrator (not public) is the natural owner of fusion. The spectrum-management slice has a single captive buyer (DISA DSO) whose data of record (JSDR) is CUI and whose sanctioned answer is EMBM-J (Palantir prototype, GEMSIS sustainment contractor); a few thousand spectrum managers is too small a user base for venture returns. Emitter libraries are classified and vendor-channelled. Existing TAK RF plugins (TEMS, TAKX-RF, ATAKRR) show the plumbing is easy, which means the value is in exercise access, accreditation and data agreements rather than code.
technical_wedge: A government-ownable TAK Server microservice plus ATAK/WinTAK plugin that ingests detections from any sensor through an open schema (SigMF metadata plus Cursor-on-Target extensions, adapters for S2AS/MOTH/Dragonfly/TLS exports as they become available), time-aligns and deduplicates them under DDIL using CRDT-style replication, renders friendly-emitter heat maps and a command-post signature score against the unit's own frequency assignments (SFAF import), and produces JSIR-format interference tickets that queue offline and sync to Spectrum XXI/EMBM-J when connected. Emitter-library distribution is out of scope for a startup (classified, vendor-owned).

mvp.what: ATAK-CIV plugin + TAK Server plugin: open detection schema, adapters for two commercial SDR sensors (KrakenSDR for AoA, USRP/RTL-SDR for occupancy), DDIL sync, friendly-emitter heat map, own-signature score versus an imported SFAF assignment list, offline JSIR-style EMI ticket queue.
mvp.demonstrable_in_3_6_months: Two-founder build on ATAK-CIV SDK: live demo at a university/ROTC or National Guard field exercise showing a command post's emission footprint, sensor-agnostic ingest from two sensor types, and picture convergence after a simulated 30-minute network outage.
mvp.what_it_must_prove: (1) that heterogeneous sensor detections fuse into one picture with acceptable false-track rate; (2) that the picture survives DDIL and reconverges; (3) that a 25E can build a JRFL/EMI ticket offline faster than with spreadsheets; (4) that PM EW&C or the EWPMT-X integrator will accept a third-party TAK microservice rather than build it.

data_requirement.what: Sensor detections (frequency, bandwidth, power, bearing, timestamps, position), unit radio/emitter inventories, frequency assignments (SFAF/JSDR records - CUI), JRFL (CUI), exercise recordings of own emissions (CUI), and eventually threat emitter parametrics (classified).
data_requirement.legally_realistically_obtainable: Own-signature and commercial-band data can be self-collected with COTS SDRs at unclassified events; SFAF-format sample data and public ATP/CJCSM documents allow synthetic assignment data; real JSDR/JRFL and vendor sensor formats require a government sponsor (CRADA, OTA or SBIR) and CUI handling under DFARS 7012; threat libraries are classified and inaccessible to an uncleared team.

entry_vehicle.eligibility_notes: SBIR/STTR requires >50% ownership and control by U.S. citizens or permanent residents (13 CFR 121.702); the Indonesian founder's shares never count and the German founder's count only after the green card, so a 50/50 split fails. CSO/OTA awards have no citizenship test but CUI and export-controlled data flow to the company on the first award; ITAR treats a lawful permanent resident as a U.S. person (22 CFR 120.62) but not the Indonesian founder. Anything marketed as EW/ES/DF for military use risks USML Category XI classification - needs export counsel before design starts.

incumbent_response.could_anduril_palantir_l3harris_add_it: Yes. Anduril's Lattice already ingests EW detections and sits in the NGC2 data baseline; Palantir holds the EMBM-J DS prototype; the EWPMT-X integrator can add fusion as a capability drop; 3dB Labs can extend S2AS to ingest other sensors under its production contract. None needs new technology to do so.
incumbent_response.why_startup_still_wins_or_reject: Weak. The only durable argument is that the Army wants a government-owned, vendor-neutral TAK component that no sensor vendor is incentivized to build, and that the incumbents' fusion is proprietary. But the Army can require that openness from 3dB Labs, Heaviside and RII contractually (REWSI already demands MOSA/APIs), which removes the startup's reason to exist. Recommend treating this as a subcontract/plugin niche, not a venture-scale company.

regulatory_burden.explanation: Software specially designed for military EW/ES/direction-finding is likely to be reviewed under USML Category XI (ITAR), triggering DDTC registration and deemed-export controls; commercial spectrum-monitoring on COTS SDRs may fall under EAR (5A001/5D001 or EAR99) depending on design intent - only a commodity jurisdiction/classification review by counsel can settle this. All DoD frequency plans, unit signatures and sensor positions are CUI from the first exercise (DFARS 252.204-7012, NIST SP 800-171, CMMC clause effective 2025-11-10). Threat emitter libraries and EWPMT-X classified integration require facility and personnel clearances (U.S. citizenship required).
regulatory_burden.non_us_person_founder_note: If the product is ITAR-controlled, sharing technical data with the Indonesian co-founder is a deemed export requiring DDTC authorization or a compartmented structure; the German founder becomes a U.S. person for ITAR only on issuance of permanent residence (22 CFR 120.62). Both founders are years from clearance eligibility. SBIR eligibility fails unless >50% of ownership/control is held by U.S. citizens/permanent residents. FOCI review (32 CFR 117.11; DoDI 5205.87 for some unclassified contracts) will surface both founders. Scoping the first product to EAR99/EAR dual-use spectrum monitoring (own-signature and interference only, no threat ID) is the usual mitigation; all of this requires specialist export-control and immigration counsel - no legal judgment made here.

dual_use_potential.explanation: Sensor-agnostic RF occupancy fusion, offline frequency-plan management and interference ticketing have civil analogues (public-safety event spectrum management, range and test-site monitoring, telecom interference hunting, regulators, airports/critical infrastructure C-UAS RF awareness), and TAK is used by DHS/CBP/public-safety agencies. But those buyers are few and price-sensitive (Aurora Insight ended in a Maxar acquisition rather than scale), so dual use reduces ITAR exposure more than it creates a large market.

defensibility.explanation: Code is not defensible (multiple TAK RF plugins exist and ATAK-CIV is open). Defensibility would come from vendor adapters negotiated with S2AS/REWSI vendors, SFAF/JSDR/EMBM-J interface agreements with DISA, TAK-GOV accreditation and ATO, exercise-derived own-signature datasets, and a 25E-validated workflow. All of these are controllable by the government and can be handed to an incumbent, so defensibility is low-to-medium at best.

why_now: 2024: Army cancelled EWPMT follow-on and fixed TAK as the EW/spectrum host (EWPMT-X), opening a plugin path. 2025-2026: S2AS moved from a ~$6.1M prototype OTA to a $350M-ceiling production contract on the UCA pathway with fielding underway; REWSI produced two production sensor IDIQs (~$196M ceilings) demanding MOSA/API/NGC2 integration; DISA launched EMBM-J DS (Apr 2025) and is recompeting EMBM-J SA; NGC2 common data baseline and Lightning Surge showed EW data must feed the common data layer. Ukraine-style signature targeting made own-signature awareness a commander-level priority. Cheap SDRs, edge compute and RF ML make sensor-agnostic fusion technically cheap for the first time.
killer_risk: The two highest-value slices were just awarded: own-signature to 3dB Labs (production, June 2026) and joint spectrum management to DISA's EMBM-J (Palantir prototype, SA recompete), while the residual fusion layer sits inside EWPMT-X scope that the Army can assign to its integrator or require from sensor vendors under REWSI's open-architecture terms; combined with likely ITAR Category XI jurisdiction, CUI-only data, a few-thousand-person user base and a non-U.S.-person co-founder, there is no venture-scale, founder-accessible company here - at most a small TAK-plugin subcontracting business.
